S031.name: Diminished_Thinking
S031.description: Diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness.

subtypes.Reduced Concentration: Unable to pay attention or maintain focus on specific activities like conversation, reading, or watching TV.
subtypes.Indecisiveness: Extreme difficulty making even minor daily choices (e.g., menu, clothes) and hesitating to make decisions.
subtypes.Subjective Memory Complaints: Complaining of memory decline, such as forgetting where things were placed, due to reduced focus.
subtypes.Clouded Thinking: Thinking feels foggy, dazed, or not clear.

S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.

subtypes.Intrusive Memories: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Distressing Dreams: Recurrent distressing dreams in which the content and/or affect of the dream are related to the traumatic event.
subtypes.Dissociative Reactions (Flashbacks): Dissociative reactions (e.g., flashbacks) in which the individual feels or acts as if the traumatic event were recurring.
subtypes.Psychological Distress at Cues: Intense or prolonged psychological distress at exposure to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Physiological Reactions to Cues: Marked physiological reactions to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.

S070.name: Trauma_Avoidance
S070.description: Persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event.

subtypes.Internal Avoidance: Efforts to avoid distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings about or closely associated with the traumatic event.
subtypes.External Avoidance: Efforts to avoid external reminders (people, places, conversations, activities, objects, situations) that arouse distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.

subtypes.Impulsive Anger: Sudden explosions of anger for trivial reasons or no clear reason.
subtypes.Verbal Aggression: Attacking others with shouting, cursing, or blame without holding back.
subtypes.Physical Aggression: Physically attacking people or throwing/breaking objects.
subtypes.Chronic Irritability: A state where nerves are always sharp and sensitive, ready to explode at the slightest touch.

S080.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
S080.description: Exaggerated startle response to minor stimuli.

subtypes.Auditory Startle: Startling excessively and flinching physically at sudden noises.
subtypes.Tactile Startle: Being extremely startled by unexpected physical contact.
subtypes.Visual Startle: Being greatly startled and wary of sudden appearances of people or rapid movements.
subtypes.Slow Recovery: Heart pounding and trembling for a long time after being startled, not calming down easily.

S082.name: Depersonalization_Derealization
S082.description: Altered sense of the reality of one's self or surroundings after a traumatic event.

subtypes.Depersonalization: Feeling detached from one's own body or mental processes, as if being an outside observer.
subtypes.Derealization: The surrounding environment feels unreal, dreamlike, distant, or distorted.
subtypes.Time Distortion: Time feels like it has stopped during the traumatic moment, or is perceived as moving extremely slowly or quickly.

symptom.disease_info: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is a trauma- and stressor-related condition that emerges within days of exposure to an event involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation, either directly, as a witness, or through learning of it occurring to a close other. It is characterized by intrusive recollections, avoidance, negative mood, dissociation, and marked arousal that last at least 3 days but less than 1 month, with clear functional impairment. Clinically, ASD often presents with sudden changes in behavior and functioning after a discrete traumatic incident, with patients describing feeling "numb," "disconnected," or constantly on edge, and struggling to resume normal routines. It is distinguished from PTSD primarily by its shorter duration and immediate temporal relationship to the trauma; persistent symptoms beyond one month suggest progression to PTSD.

patient.personality: A methodical, health-conscious construction manager who is both detail-focused and assertive, with a strong sense of responsibility for her crews.
patient.stressor: Jasmine was overseeing a concrete pour at a flood-zone construction site in Houston when a sudden scaffolding failure caused a partial collapse, pinning one of her longtime crew members and narrowly missing several others standing near her. She had done multiple safety walk-throughs that morning and initially stayed composed to coordinate emergency services, but the realization that someone under her supervision was critically injured on her watch hit her hard afterward. In the two weeks that followed, she forced herself back to work yet found her usual confidence shaken; routine site noises like nail guns or dropped lumber made her jerk and lose her train of thought during briefings, and she started avoiding walking under any temporary structures, delegating field checks she used to do personally. When her startled reactions and hesitancy began to unsettle her crew and she found herself dreading simple site visits despite her commitment to the project, her husband and a trusted colleague urged her to get a professional evaluation through the company’s occupational health provider.
patient.chief_complaint: “Ever since that collapse, every little bang or sudden noise on site makes me jump out of my skin, and it’s starting to mess with how I do my job.”

S031.name: Diminished_Thinking
S031.description: Diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness.
S031.manifestation: Since the accident, it’s like my brain is full of static—I'll be in the middle of a safety briefing or writing an email and just lose my train of thought, staring at the screen or the guys waiting for me to finish my sentence and not knowing what I was about to say.

S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
S069.manifestation: All day long these little clips of the collapse pop into my head out of nowhere—the screech of the metal, seeing him pinned, thinking, ‘this is on me’—and at night I either dream I’m back on that site or wake up sweating because I hear that cracking sound in my sleep.

S070.name: Trauma_Avoidance
S070.description: Persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event.
S070.manifestation: I catch myself doing laps around the site to avoid walking anywhere near scaffolding or temporary supports, and I shut down any conversation that starts drifting toward what happened because the second I start to picture it, I feel like I’m going to fall apart.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.
S077.manifestation: I’ve been snapping at people over nothing—if a worker asks the same question twice or my husband suggests I take a day off, I just explode, raising my voice and saying things I don’t mean, then feel awful about it afterward.

S080.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
S080.description: Exaggerated startle response to minor stimuli.
S080.manifestation: Now every time a nail gun fires, a pallet drops, or someone yells unexpectedly, I physically jolt, my heart slams in my chest, and it takes a few minutes of deep breathing before I can refocus on whatever I was supposed to be doing.

S082.name: Depersonalization_Derealization
S082.description: Altered sense of the reality of one's self or surroundings after a traumatic event.
S082.manifestation: There are moments on site, especially near where the collapse happened, when everything feels weirdly far away and muffled, like I’m watching myself walk around and give orders in a movie instead of actually being there.
